name: Black tie dressing

lead: Black tie is a semi-formal Western evening dress code built around a dinner jacket, white dress shirt, black bow tie and formal shoes. It sits below white tie and above business dress.
A well-fitted tuxedo is widely regarded as flattering because the dark jacket, lapel line and crisp shirt frame the torso, which is why it appears in looks and style discussions.

paras: Men wear a black or midnight blue dinner jacket with satin or grosgrain lapel facings, braided-seam trousers, a white shirt, a self-tie bow tie, a waistcoat or cummerbund, and black formal shoes. It is traditionally worn after 6 p.m.
Few risks beyond cost and fit; invitations can specify variants such as white dinner jackets in warm climates.

angle.text: The dress code prescribes a set of garments that frame the torso with a defined lapel and shirt front. Fit and tailoring determine how it reads on the wearer.

lead: Black tie is a semi-formal Western evening dress code, called dinner suit or dinner jacket in British English and tuxedo in American English. [1] It is traditionally worn after 6 p.m. and ranks below white tie and above business dress. [1]
People use it to present a sharp, polished appearance at formal events; the standard components are a tailless dinner jacket, white shirt, bow tie and formal footwear. [1]

paras: Traditional men's black tie comprises a single-breasted black or midnight blue jacket with satin or grosgrain lapels, trousers with a braid stripe and no belt loops, a white shirt with turndown collar and double cuffs, a self-tie black bow tie, a waistcoat or cummerbund, studs and cufflinks, black socks and patent court shoes or plain oxfords. [1] Women wear evening gowns, ball gowns or cocktail dresses, and Yves Saint Laurent's Le Smoking (1966) introduced a women's dinner suit. [1]

The earliest record of a tailless evening jacket is a midnight blue smoking jacket ordered by the Prince of Wales from Henry Poole & Co. in 1865. [1] The style reached Tuxedo Park, New York, around 1886 and was widely accepted by 1888. [1] A black waistcoat and bow tie became convention in the Edwardian era, and after the 1960s black tie increasingly replaced white tie in the US. [1]
It is worn at balls, galas, dinner parties, proms, some weddings, cruise formal dinners, formal debates at some British university societies, and by male musicians at concerts. [1]
